ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Progress Note 5 — Focused Visit (Follow-up) — Howard Hughes — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Ten-week review: sertraline to an OCD dose, exposure therapy and his staff's part in it, hearing aids and pain

text.paragraph: Ten-week review: sertraline dose, exposure therapy, his staff's part, hearing aids and pain. [S]

Mr. Hughes returns five weeks after his five-week review. The nurse called two weeks after the dose increase, and sertraline 100 mg has caused only mild sweating at night. His bronchitis from the sick visit cleared within three weeks without antibiotics. He has had nine exposure sessions in all, now twice weekly; he eats food his cook prepares without watching, and he has shaken hands twice at work. His assistant has attended two sessions, and the staff no longer wrap objects in tissue or wash before handing him things; he still asks for sealed milk bottles. Washing and checking take about two hours a day. He has used no opioid other than buprenorphine. Today, with his therapist waiting outside, he used the clinic bathroom and gave a urine sample. His hearing aids were fitted this morning. [S]

tr.td: Well; blood pressure 116/74, pulse 74; weight 74.6 kg, BMI 20.4

Intrusive fears of contamination by germs for about a year, worse since the crash, with hand washing, cleaning of objects and avoidance of handshakes, shared spaces and food handled by others, taking about four hours a day; he recognizes the fears are probably excessive; cause under evaluation
S — Synthetic presenting problem anchored to his documented fear of germs; resolved into the diagnosis of OCD at the consultation. Not a claim about his real symptoms in 1947.
Obsessive-compulsive disorder, contamination type, with good or fair insight, not tic-related; Y-BOCS 28 (severe) at intake; no post-traumatic stress disorder on screening
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis made at the consultation, linked to the retrospective interpretation of his documented fears (R). Not a claim about his real diagnosis.

Opioid use disorder, moderate (four of the DSM-5-TR criteria that count for a prescribed opioid: taking more than prescribed, failed attempts to cut down, time spent getting prescriptions from two prescribers, and craving), on codeine prescribed after a crash; buprenorphine planned
S — Synthetic modern coding; tolerance and withdrawal are not counted for a medicine taken under medical supervision. Person-first language; not a claim about his real diagnosis.
Chronic pain after major trauma ten months ago (crushed chest with rib fractures, collapsed lung, other fractures and burns): chest wall, left shoulder and low back pain, PEG 6.7
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis anchored to his documented injuries.
Difficulty hearing conversation, worse in noise, after years of flying in loud aircraft; cause under evaluation

S — Synthetic acute illness; not a historical claim.

Obsessive-compulsive disorder, partial response (F42.2). Y-BOCS 19, a 32 percent fall after five weeks at 100 mg: a partial response. The APA guideline supports raising the dose toward the top of the range before judging the trial; augmentation is held in reserve until he has had 8 to 12 weeks at the highest dose he tolerates. Safety reviewed: no thoughts of suicide or of harming anyone. [S]
Sertraline 200 mg daily.

Continue buprenorphine; dispensed four weeks at a time.

Audiologist review in one month.

text.paragraph: Guideline basis: Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (2007); Guideline Watch (March 2013): Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (Koran LM, Simpson HB), as reported by Psychiatric News (2013); Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment (CG31) (2005); CDC Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing Opioids for Pain - United States, 2022 (2022); The ASAM National Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Opioid Use Disorder: 2020 Focused Update (2020); Prescription Drug Monitoring Programs (PDMPs) (2026); Hearing loss in adults: assessment and management (NG98) (2018); VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide (2024); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monograph (2026)

Follow-up: Nurse telephone call in two weeks. Preventive visit in about two months. Twenty-two-week review in about twelve weeks with laboratory tests. Call the clinic or 988 at any time. Next scheduled visit 1947-09-14: periodic adult preventive visit. [S]
